# 13-aircaps: sources

Back-test entry `13-aircaps.yaml`. AirCaps, YC Fall 2025 (Launch YC 2025-11-05). Read 2026-10-22.

Sources (short names used below):

- **SITE**: https://www.aircaps.com (testimonials, pricing, how it works)
- **YC-L**: Launch YC post. https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/Olk-aircaps-the-ai-copilot-for-in-person-conversations
- **YC-C**: YC company page. https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/aircaps
- **YALE**: Yale Alumni Magazine. https://yalealumnimagazine.org/articles/6208
- **SD**: Stanford Daily, 2023-02-06 (TranscribeGlass). https://stanforddaily.com/2023/02/06/stanford-startup-transcribeglass-seeks-to-bring-ease-and-affordability-to-assistive-technology/
- **SMI**: Smithsonian Magazine. https://www.smithsonianmag.com/innovation/this-augmented-reality-tool-could-change-communication-for-some-deaf-and-hearing-impaired-people-180982996/
- **T4G**: Tech4Good Awards finalist entry. https://tech4goodawards.com/finalist/transcribeglass/ (quoted through the shortlist; not re-fetched)
- **HT**: HearingTracker, "Hear with Your Eyes: A Review of Live Captioning Glasses". https://www.hearingtracker.com/hearing-glasses/hear-with-your-eyes-five-ar-live-captioning-glasses
- **DTS-ASL**: ASL Deafined blog, "Dinner Table Syndrome: What Deaf, DeafBlind, and Hard of Hearing People Face". https://blog.asldeafined.com/2025/05/dinner-table-syndrome-what-deaf-deafblind-and-hard-of-hearing-people-face/

**Caution:** the origin story comes from the founder's earlier device, TranscribeGlass (about 2017 to 2023), which predates the YC batch. Here it is the founder's own account of where the problem came from, not evidence about AirCaps' buyers.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (the CONSUMER role, `wearer`; context actor).**
- T4G (through the shortlist): a hard-of-hearing friend who "dropped out of school because day-to-day communication with other students was becoming an insurmountable problem".
- SMI: the friend "found it difficult to understand what teachers and even his friends were saying."
- YALE: the founder began at 16, after a hard-of-hearing classmate in Delhi left school because hearing aids alone did not let him follow his teachers (as read).
- SITE, "Who it's for": "Deaf and Hard of Hearing people" first, then travelers, multilingual families and professionals.

**2. What (the job).**
- YC-L: phones break eye contact and earbuds confuse the audio (as read), so face-to-face conversations get no captions.
- SITE: a private display in the lenses shows the text, visible only to the wearer (as read).
- Job wording ("follow and join a face-to-face conversation") is mine, from these two.

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "When I was sitting around a table, I lost the conversation".
- SD (co-founder with hearing loss): "my understanding drops to 20% at best" in group conversations, where he mostly nods along.
- SMI: "Hearing aids aren't dependable in a lot of situations, especially ones with a lot of background noise."
- *My choice:* occasion "group conversation"; window 7 days; Frequency 4 to 7 days out of 7. That rests on YC-L's power users (6+ hours of daily use, as read) and the ordinary weekly rhythm of meals, work and family.

**4. Which people (segment, market).**
- SITE lists deaf and hard-of-hearing people first. YC-L also names meeting-heavy professionals.
- YALE: a Deaf ASL instructor who does not speak sees the glasses as one-directional.
- *My choice:* the segment is narrowed to "deaf and hard-of-hearing adults in the US who talk with hearing people every week". This is the day-one wedge the origin story points at, and the travellers and professionals came later. Market US: the testimonials and HSA/FSA are US.

**5. Who pays (Buyer and payer).**
- SITE: "HSA/FSA eligible" (as read). One testimonial is from a daughter about her father joining family conversations.
- *My choice:* the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree (Nobody else, picked).

**6. Mechanism (solution statement, solution_mechanism, compatibility and adoption items).**
- YC-L: captions and notes "displayed on lightweight AR glasses" (as read).
- SITE: four microphones capture nearby speech; the glasses "require a Bluetooth connection to a phone and an internet connection" (as read).
- Compatibility tests "Their phone was with them and online", because the mechanism needs both. Adoption friction tests "Wear the glasses, paired to the phone". Both are my choices from these facts.
- Commitment step "order a pair with free returns": SITE, "15-day risk-free returns".

**7. Price (Price, Existing sacrifice, Ability to pay).**
- SITE: glasses "Starting at $599"; free plan with unlimited captions; "Pro plan: $20/month".
- YALE: "which cost $649 in early 2026". HT's table: "$499 / $699 (Premium $20/mth)".
- *My choice:* the price is put on a year, because the ladder has no one-off: **$599 to $839 a year**. That is the glasses with free captions, up to the glasses plus twelve months of Pro.
- *My choice:* the cost estimate (Existing sacrifice) is **$200 to $1,500 a year**, from the commercial statement's "many already pay for captioning apps and hearing-aid extras". No source gives a figure. SMI notes hearing aids are "often costing thousands of dollars", so the high end stops short of a hearing aid itself. Ability to pay is derived by code: 40% to 420%, some from spend.

**8. Occasions (statements, gate, stories).**
- SITE testimonials: "I could start going to the theatre again"; "With AirCaps I can follow almost all" (at a table with friends); "I can attend speeches and seminars in large spaces and understand words"; a testimonial about an uncaptioned movie theater; one about a father following family conversations.
- Shortlist reading of SITE: "My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups".
- YALE: a first-year deaf in one ear followed three friends in a noisy café. A largely deaf professor found the captions "messing up" at a screening, and they kept him in the loop on a walk drowned by construction noise.

## The respondents

No respondent carries a real person's name; every name is invented. Where a story follows a public account, the occasion is borrowed and the person is not.

- Harriet Coleman: SITE theatre testimonial ("I could start going to the theatre again").
- Walter Nguyen: shortlist reading of SITE ("My wife appreciates not having to repeat or explain for me in groups") and the SITE family-conversation testimonial.
- Diego Herrera: SITE table-with-friends testimonial; DTS-ASL ("if others are facing away or talking too quickly, these visual cues can be lost").
- Amaka Obi: YC-L (phones break eye contact); SMI (phone subtitles leave users "stuck looking at their screens at all times"); SITE work testimonial.
- Ruth Feldman: SITE testimonial on "speeches and seminars in large spaces".
- Tomás Reyes: YALE, the first-year deaf in one ear with three friends in a café.
- Eleanor Park: YALE, the campus walk where construction noise nearly drowned the conversation.
- Colette Marchand: SITE testimonial on an uncaptioned movie theater; YALE screening.
- Andrea Whitlock: YALE, the Deaf ASL instructor who sees the glasses as one-directional and worries institutions could cut services. She is the sceptic who will not adopt.
- Gordon McBride: author's invention, filling a gap: a hearing-aid user whose quiet week went fine, the low-frequency case. It is the other side of SMI's "aren't dependable ... with a lot of background noise".
- Kwame Asante: SD (bars: "I have a really hard time"; "my understanding drops to 20% at best", nodding along).
- Shirin Tehrani: SMI, the late-deafened user who relies "completely on live transcription and captions" and names doctor visits.
- Beatriz Souza: SMI ("Since the app needs the speaker to converse in English, I have not been able to use it much in social settings").
- Hollis Grant: author's invention, filling a gap: a vague, unanchored story so the entry carries one GUESSED reading.
- Naomi Adler: author's invention, filling a gap: a chipped story (rather not say). DTS-ASL on "frustration, anxiety, and even a reluctance to attend social events".
- Frank Dellinger: DTS-ASL (family dinners and gatherings, "talking over each other").
- Ingrid Solberg: author's invention, filling a gap: a counter conversation through a screen and a mask, where lipreading fails. DTS-ASL on lost visual cues.
- Patrick Moran: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No (a quiet week with no hard conversation).
- Lucia Ferraro: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.
- Desmond Hale: author's invention, filling a gap: gate No.

## Open

- **The origin story predates the batch.** It is TranscribeGlass's. The day-one founder statements use it as the founders do in the press, but a back-test should weigh it as the founder's lived reason, not as customer evidence.
- **Price conflict.** SITE says $599, YALE $649 (early 2026), and HT $499 / $699. I used SITE's $599, as the price the founder would type today. The year framing ($599 to $839) is mine.
- **The cost estimate is mine.** $200 to $1,500 a year has no public figure behind it. The commercial vector's NOT_HOLDING_UP comes mostly from people who spend nothing today (free phone captions), against that estimate.
- **Two shortlist quotes not re-seen.** My fetch of SITE did not return the "sitting around a table, I lost the conversation" and "My wife appreciates..." quotes verbatim, though it did return the other testimonials. They are cited through the shortlist. The site may rotate testimonials.
- **Relative advantage code.** keel-cloud's `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` accepts only five legacy advantage codes. The benefit is labelled "Following more without asking anyone to repeat" under the nearest code, `less_help_needed`.
- **Checker result.** `instructions/corpus.py` (keel-e2e-eval) loads the file with the registry bound and raises no refusal. `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` reports only "missing top-level 'expected'", which is intentional. Its recount, which is not a golden: PROBLEM PEOPLE_DISAGREE (Frequency: many have it 2 to 3 days a week, not 4 to 7), SOLUTION HOLDING_UP, COMMERCIAL NOT_HOLDING_UP (Existing sacrifice).

screens.why2: The words are plain, but the same person appears on two rows and the intro repeats the title, so I had to read it twice to see these were one wearer and not two people.
screens.why3: Who buys AirCaps is my own business: the wearer orders it, often with HSA/FSA money, and nobody signs off.
screens.why4: The two 'Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult' rows overlap, since it is one person who both has the problem and decides, and the 'Nobody else' row has no tag.
screens.why5: It keeps what I said: the wearer decides and pays, and nobody else has to agree, with no role added.
screens.why7: The card says the person with the problem and the decider share one row when they are the same person, and that every row carries a tag; here the wearer is split across two rows and 'Nobody else' is untagged, though the belief that nobody else has to agree still matches my answer.
screens.instead: The people involved: Deaf or hard-of-hearing adult · has the problem and decides to buy / Nobody else · has to agree

screens.why1: Right after I checked the who-has-to-agree list, it is natural to confirm the belief, and since I named only Nobody else it rightly turns into a statement to confirm rather than a pick.
screens.why2: The belief reads plainly, but the bar's 'the last time they paid for something for this' is clumsy and needs a second read; it should say 'something like this'.
screens.why3: Whether my wearers decide and pay alone is something I know from my own customers: HSA/FSA, a pair ordered direct with free returns.
screens.why4: With only Nobody else on the list there is no false choice, just continue or go back to name someone, and both ways out fit.
screens.why5: I picked Nobody else, and the screen tests exactly that: the wearer decides, and nobody else must agree first.
screens.why7: Nobody else is tested as a statement to confirm, as the card says, and the bar counts only 'decided alone' as support, so it can be both supported and refuted.
screens.instead: Keep the screen, but word the bar as: Holds if at least 2 in 3 deaf or hard-of-hearing adults say nobody else had to agree the last time they paid for something like this.

screens.why1: Once I've said who pays and what it costs, asking what first step I'd want a deaf or hard-of-hearing adult to take before paying is the obvious next commercial question.
screens.why2: The question, the 9-word limit and the note about a smaller free step are plain to me, though the examples 'pay for a pilot' and 'let us run a trial' read like a B2B sale, not someone buying glasses for their own dinners.
screens.why3: I know exactly what I want a wearer to do first, because ordering with our 15-day risk-free returns is how people start with AirCaps today.
screens.why4: It's a box to type in with only the 'I'm not sure' chip, which fits because the card lets the founder leave this dimension out.
screens.why5: My answer 'order the caption glasses with free returns' sits whole at 7 words, with 'free returns' and the product kept, and nothing is reworded on this screen.
screens.why7: The box asks for one first step of up to 9 words, says where any money goes, and promises a smaller free step on the next screen when the step costs money, data or a signature, which is exactly the card's founder shape. Ordering costs money, so that smaller step will be drafted.
screens.instead: Same question, but with examples a consumer founder would recognise, e.g. "order a pair with free returns" or "download the free app and try it".

screens.why1: Right after I typed my first step and what it costs, it makes sense to check how strangers will hear the step and what they can answer to it.
screens.why2: The four answers read plainly to deaf and hard-of-hearing adults, but the smaller-step line I am meant to keep or change says 'Yes, after try a pair of caption glasses first', which is ungrammatical and makes me read it twice.
screens.why3: Whether they would order glasses with a 15-day free return is a buying decision my wearers make themselves, often with HSA/FSA money.
screens.why4: The options are complete and run firm to soft, but 'after trying a pair first' sits close to the step itself, since free returns already is how most people try a pair; it only stands apart if they picture a demo before ordering.
screens.why5: 'Order the caption glasses with free returns' keeps my step and its returnable term, and nothing about my roles leaks to the wearer.
screens.why7: The served list meets the card: the step whole first, a soft yes on a free smaller step, then Probably not and No, with no escape and a belief that can be both supported and refuted; but the drafted smaller step is not the noun phrase the card asks for ('Yes, after try ...'), and the 'trying a pair' smaller step half-overlaps the free-returns step.
screens.instead: Smaller step: 'trying a pair at a demo first'. Options: Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after trying a pair at a demo first · Probably not · No.

screens.why1: Right after I named the first real step (order the caption glasses with free returns), asking whether to invite people to take it is the obvious next move before the study goes out.
screens.why2: Short and plain, and the hint says exactly what the respondent will see and where I find the yeses.
screens.why3: Whether I want a list of deaf and hard-of-hearing people ready to try the glasses is my own call and easy to make.
screens.why4: Yes or no is the complete choice here, and both options are clear and distinct.
screens.why5: My step was ordering the glasses with free returns, but the line people see says 'try this for real' and asks for an email, which is softer than ordering; the screen doesn't show me how my step will be worded to them.
screens.instead: Offer a pilot? People who say yes see: "Would you order the caption glasses with free 15-day returns? Leave your email." — Yes, ask them / No pilot

screens.why1: Picking who asks the questions belongs here, just before strangers see the study, after the pilot offer.
screens.why2: Two names, a five-second sample and a credit cost are plain to me on first read.
screens.why3: I can judge a voice, but my people mostly lipread or read, so what I'd actually judge is how clear her face and mouth are and whether the questions are captioned, and a 'Hear' sample doesn't show me that.
screens.why4: Daphne and Saskia are distinct, but for deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents the choice I'd want is missing: a preview of the face and captions, or a text-only interviewer with no voice at all.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or my roles leaks into the interviewer choice, and the hint keeps that every question is written on screen and can be answered by typing or tapping.
screens.instead: Who should ask your questions? Every question is captioned on screen. Options: Daphne (▶ watch 5 s, captioned), Saskia (▶ watch 5 s, captioned), Text only, no video.

screens.why1: Near the end of the flow, after choosing who asks the questions, it is the obvious next thing to decide how my deaf and hard-of-hearing respondents will answer.
screens.why2: Video, typing, tapping and speaking into a box are plain to me, and the line that every question is also written on the screen answers the first thing I'd worry about for a deaf audience.
screens.why3: I know my people: many read captions all day and some sign rather than speak, so I can choose this from what I know of them.
screens.why4: Text, AI video with on-screen text, or let them choose covers the real choices without overlap, and the true answer for my wearers, Read and tap, is there.
screens.why5: It names the people the way I typed them, deaf or hard-of-hearing adults, and nothing of AirCaps or the glasses leaks into how they answer.

screens.why1: After choosing how people answer, the last thing before sending is who gets the link, so it sits exactly where I'd expect it.
screens.why2: Know them by name, a list from a search, or one open link posted in a group: plain words I'd answer on first read.
screens.why3: I know who I can reach: the hard-of-hearing users I already know and the online groups for deaf and hard-of-hearing people where I'd post a link.
screens.why4: The three routes are distinct and cover my real ways to reach people, but making every person in an open group sign in with Google is a hurdle I wouldn't have chosen, and it's dropped on me here without warning.
screens.why5: Nothing of AirCaps or my roles is altered or leaks here; my pick of people I know by name is kept as I made it.
screens.instead: Who gets a link? -- People I know by name (I send each their own link) / A list I found with Keel / One open link I post in a group, such as a deaf and hard-of-hearing forum (each person signs in before the interview)

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right under the title with its deciding number, 1 of 7 losing 12 or more conversations a month, though Price's 0 of 7 looks like the harder miss to me and the line names only Existing sacrifice.
screens.why_b2: Each card shows what is counted, over 7 people, and the bar of 5 of 7 plainly, and the tally of 2 holding, 2 not holding and 1 not reached reads at a glance; only the numbering skip from 4 to 6 made me look twice.
screens.why_b3: Price, Buyer and payer and Commitment are mine, but I put Existing sacrifice in at $200 to $1,500 a year and here it is about 12 lost conversations a month, so I recognise it without it being my words.
screens.why_b4: The status lines say they lose less than I thought and value it below $599, but nothing tells me what to try next, such as what price they did name or whether to lead with the free tier and a cheaper pair.
screens.why_b5: The 7 respondents stay visible on every card and nothing is called strong, but no line says 7 is a small sample to call 'Holding up' or 'Not holding up' on.
screens.instead: Not holding up on price: 0 of 7 would pay $599 and most lose fewer than 12 conversations a month; with only 7 people, find out what they would pay before cutting the price or leading with the free plan.

screens.why_b1: The verdict reads Not holding up, and right beside it is the deciding count: 1 of 7 at 12 or more against a bar of 5 of 7.
screens.why_b2: The headcount and the bar are plain, but the unit reads 'conversations of the conversations they are in a month', which sounds like a share, and a marker at 5 on a 0 to 15 conversation axis looks like 5 conversations, so I had to read it twice.
screens.why_b3: I recognise my 12 conversations a month, but 'Deaf or hard-of-hearing adults already lose ... conversations they lost the thread of' says lose twice and isn't how I'd put my people in the plural.
screens.why_b4: The So line restates the count and points me to the Price card, but it never says what a lower count means for my pitch, such as selling on which conversations matter rather than how many go wrong.
screens.why_b5: All 7 are visible, the count line calls it a small group and a lean rather than a call, and nothing claims more than these 7 show.
screens.instead: Deaf and hard-of-hearing adults already lose the thread of about 12 conversations a month. Not holding up: 6 of 7 said fewer, mostly 2 to 8, against a bar of 5 of 7. A lean from 7 people: the count may be lower than you think, so price on which conversations matter, not how many.

screens.why_b1: The verdict 'Not holding up' sits right beside the deciding numbers: 0 of 7 at $599 or more up front, 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month, against a bar of 5 of 7 on each.
screens.why_b2: Each of the two ladders shows its count per band over 7 people, marks my $599 and my $20 at a band's low edge, and draws the 5 of 7 bar, so what is counted, over whom and where the bar sits are plain at once.
screens.why_b3: The belief is my price as I set it: AirCaps, $599 up front, then the optional $20 a month plan, said of deaf and hard-of-hearing adults.
screens.why_b4: The So line tells me 6 of 7 clustered at $250 to under $599, which is useful, but it then says only 'fewer than 2 in 3' when the count is 0 of 7, and it sends me to another tab instead of naming a move; the trial-first quotes point to one, such as leading with the 15-day returns or testing a price under $599.
screens.why_b5: Every claim stays inside the 7 who answered, and the count line itself flags 'a small group: a lean, not a call', so nothing overreaches.
screens.instead: None of 7 would pay $599 up front, but 6 of 7 put it just under, at $250 to $599, and several want to try a pair first: test a price under $599 or lead with the free-returns trial, and with 7 people treat this as a lean.

screens.why_b1: 'Not reached' sits right beside '0 of 7 named your price or more · nothing to ask', so I know the verdict and the number behind it at once.
screens.why_b2: Three bars at 0 and the count line 'not asked: 7 named less' make clear nobody was counted, but the strip shows 5 ghost cells against 7 people and the 2-in-3 bar is never drawn or named, so I have to look twice to see what the ghosts and the bar mean.
screens.why_b3: The price ($599 up front, optional $20 a month) is mine and the belief is recognisable, but I never typed or checked a 'money they already spend' belief, and the card does not say Keel derived it from my cost and price.
screens.why_b4: 'Ability to pay waits until at least 5 do' only says the card is on hold; it doesn't tell me the blocker is the Price result, where everyone sat below $599 and most below $20 a month.
screens.why_b5: No claim goes beyond the 7: it says nothing was asked and decides nothing, though 'Only 0 of 7' reads oddly.
screens.instead: Not reached: none of the 7 named $599 or more (5 said $250 to $599, most under $10 a month), so nobody was asked where the money would come from; settle Price first, by testing a lower up-front price or a cheaper entry pair, before this can be read.

screens.why_b1: The card says 'Holding up' with '6 of 7 decided alone · bar 5 of 7' right beside it, so I know the belief held and by how much it cleared the bar.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts who had to agree last time, over 7 people, with 6 for and 1 against, and the marker sits at 5 of 7; I took all of that in on first look.
screens.why_b3: 'Buyer and payer' and 'The deaf or hard-of-hearing adult decides, and nobody else must agree first' are my pick, Nobody else, in my wearer's words.
screens.why_b4: The So line only restates the count; it doesn't tell me to sell straight to the wearer, and it doesn't note that the Price card says nobody would pay $599 anyway, so who signs off isn't what's blocking me.
screens.why_b5: All 7 are shown, the count line says 'a small group: a lean, not a call', and the one against (Walter) is named, so nothing claims more than seven people can carry.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 paid alone last time, so sell to the wearer directly with no one else to win over; but the Price card says none of them would pay $599, so who signs off isn't what's stopping you.

screens.why_b1: Holding up sits right beside 6 of 7 said yes against a bar of 5 of 7, so I know it held and which number decided it.
screens.why_b2: The chart counts answers to the order question over 7 people, with 6 for and 1 against, and the marker sits plainly at 5 of 7.
screens.why_b3: Commitment and 'order the caption glasses with free returns' are my step as I kept it, though the rule line's 'probably, after try a pair' is a grammar slip and the tacked-on '— if it were offered today' repeats the question.
screens.why_b4: 'Book them into it' is a generic push that doesn't fit an order of glasses, and it says nothing about the Price card two screens back, where 0 of 7 would pay $599, so I don't know whether this yes survives the price.
screens.why_b5: The count line rightly calls 7 people a lean, not a call, but the So line then gives a firm 'Book them into it' off a yes to a question that never named the price, which overstates what 6 of 7 can carry.
screens.instead: 6 of 7 would order with free returns, a lean from 7 people; the question named no price and none of them valued it at $599, so offer the order to these six with the price shown and see who still says yes.

screens.why_b1: The box opens on 'Not holding up' with '0 of 7 at $599 or more, once · then: 0 of 7 at $20 or more a month · bar 5 of 7 on each' right beside it, so I know the answer and the number that decides it.
screens.why_b3: The dimension is Price and the belief line is mine: $599 up front, then an optional $20 a month plan.
screens.why_b4: The group names hint at moves, such as a demo before buying and handling many voices, but the screen never says what the miss means for my price, for example that most answers sit at $250 to $599 and under $10 a month.
screens.why_b5: The n stays visible (7 against, 6 asked here, Amaka never saw it), each group carries its count of 2, and nothing is claimed beyond those people.
screens.why_b6: I learned that people want to try a pair before ordering even though I offer 15-day returns, that keeping up with many voices in big rooms is what would raise the value, that a one-sided user gets by with seat choice, and that a monthly fee feels heavy for casual social use.
screens.instead: Most of the 7 would pay $250 to $599 up front and under $10 a month; two want to try a pair before ordering, so lead with the 15-day returns or a demo; two would pay more if it kept up with many voices in big groups.

screens.why1: As the first screen it checks straight away whether I am someone who talks with hearing people, which is the whole point of the study.
screens.why2: Plain words I use myself; I know at once what it means and answer on first hearing.
screens.why3: I talk with hearing people at work, in shops and with family every week, so I know the answer without guessing.
screens.why4: Yes and No cover it, they do not overlap, and a gate question needs no escape.
screens.why5: It keeps the founder's every-week condition in everyday words and nothing of any product leaks to me.
screens.why6: The question is short and easy to hear, but the spoken form drops the template's closing 'Yes or no.' so I am not told the two answers aloud.
screens.instead: Do you talk with hearing people every week? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after I said I talk with hearing people every week, showing me the idea is the obvious next step before asking what I think of it.
screens.why2: Live captions, glasses, eye contact: these are words I use every day; the only slip is 'When the people nearby are talking, you wear it', which reads as if I'd put the glasses on only once talking starts, but I still get it first time.
screens.why3: Losing eye contact while I look down at a captioning app on my phone is exactly my life, so I can judge this from what I do every week.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options shown.
screens.why5: It's a deliberate idea card in plain words; nothing reaches me in a term I wouldn't use, and it says what the product does and what its makers believe.
screens.why6: Four short sentences with no parentheses, slashes or numbers, easy to take in once, though I'd be reading the on-screen card rather than hearing it.
screens.instead: Imagine AirCaps, an app on lightweight glasses that shows live captions inside the lens. You wear the glasses, and when people nearby talk, it writes out what they say as they say it. The people building it believe it would let you read the words while keeping eye contact.

screens.why1: After the idea card, asking how often conversations got away from me last month is an obvious way to find out what the problem already costs me.
screens.why2: "Stop following the thread of" ends on a dangling "of" and took me a second read, though "lose the thread" is something I'd say myself.
screens.why3: I have dozens of conversations with hearing people a month and drift out of plenty, so I'd be guessing at a count rather than recalling one.
screens.why4: A number box labelled conversations last month, with None and I can't recall, covers every true answer without overlap.
screens.why5: It asks about conversations I couldn't keep up with in plain words, with nothing of the product or any company jargon showing through.
screens.why6: The question is short, but it ends on "of" and the added fragment "A number of conversations last month" sounds clunky heard once, or read once on captions.
screens.why7: The box counts conversations a month, matching a count of conversations lost, so any number can fall below or above the founder's low; None is 0 and I can't recall is the one escape.
screens.instead: Last month, about how many conversations could you no longer follow? [ box ] conversations last month · None · I can't recall

screens.why1: Asking what AirCaps is worth fits once I've seen the idea, but it comes straight after one question about my conversations, under a 'What you do today' heading that doesn't match a price question, so it feels abrupt.
screens.why2: 'Up front' and 'a month' are how I'd talk about paying for glasses and a captioning subscription, and I can answer on first reading.
screens.why3: I've priced hearing aids and paid for caption apps, so I know what live captions in my glasses would be worth to me.
screens.why4: The bands are complete and distinct, but '$599' sits oddly among round numbers and reads like someone's sticker price rather than a band I'd think in.
screens.why5: Nothing of the founder's roles reaches me, but the $599 edge hints at a price already set, which drifts a little from a neutral ask.
screens.why6: Each step reads four short options and then a two-choice follow-up, which I could hold and answer if it came through as captions or text.
screens.why7: Both ladders are on one measure (dollars up front, then dollars a month), with six rungs each, 'I wouldn't pay for this' last, a band edge at the founder's price, bands on both sides so the belief can be supported or refuted, and the single 'I can't say' escape.
screens.instead: What would AirCaps be worth to you up front? Under $250 · $250 to under $600 · $600 to under $1,000 · $1,000 to under $2,500 · $2,500 or more · I wouldn't pay for this · I can't say

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on AirCaps, asking what would make it worth more is the obvious next question.
screens.why2: It reads my own answer back as a plain dollar range, 'about $250 to $600 up front', and asks one clear thing.
screens.why3: I know exactly what would make it worth more to me, like keeping up in a noisy restaurant or a group where people talk over each other, so I can answer from my own week.
screens.why4: A box to type in, no options.
screens.why5: AirCaps is the name from the idea card I was shown on purpose, and nothing else of the founder's plan or terms reaches me.
screens.why6: Two short sentences, one question, and the dollar range says easily aloud.

screens.why1: Right after I put a price on AirCaps, it makes sense to ask whether I'd be buying something like it on my own, the way I bought my hearing aids.
screens.why2: Short, everyday words; on first read I know it means did my husband, my audiologist or my insurance have to say yes.
screens.why3: I've paid for hearing aids and a captioning phone myself, so I know exactly who had a say.
screens.why4: The four run cleanly from me alone to someone else deciding, none overlap, and I can't say fits if I've never bought anything like it.
screens.why5: Nothing about the company's plans or its own names for people comes through; it just asks about my last purchase.
screens.why6: One short question and four short options I could hold if it were captioned or read to me; switching I to You in the spoken list is natural.
screens.why7: With nobody else being tested, the four run in order from decided alone to someone else's call, the second says someone else, the options are on the one measure, and I can't say sits apart as the escape.

screens.why1: After asking what it would be worth and who has to agree, it makes sense to finish by asking whether I'd actually order the glasses.
screens.why2: Caption glasses and free returns are both plain to me; I'd answer on the first read.
screens.why3: I buy my own hearing gear and know whether I'd order something like this to try, so I can answer from my own life.
screens.why4: The second option overlaps the first: ordering with free returns already is how I'd try a pair, and I can't picture where else I'd try one, so the soft yes blurs into the firm yes.
screens.why5: AirCaps and the glasses come from the idea card shown on purpose; nothing of the founder's plan or terms reaches me in words I wouldn't use.
screens.why6: It is one question with four short spoken options I can hold, though 'caption glasses' is said three times.
screens.why7: The shape is right: the step is said whole in the first yes, then a soft yes, probably not, and no, with no escape; but the smaller step, trying a pair, sits too close to ordering with free returns to clearly cost less, so the soft yes bends toward being the step again.
screens.instead: If it were ready today, would you order the caption glasses with free returns, or not? Yes, I'd order the caption glasses with free returns · Probably, after a free try-on in person first · Probably not · No
